taxonomy_heading.text: OmniTaskonomy: A Unified Taxonomy of Visual Capabilities

source.raw_tex: \section{\methodname: A Unified Taxonomy of Visual Capabilities}

taxonomy_lead.text: We introduce OmniTaskonomy, a shared hierarchy that organizes I2I supervision objectives and I2T evaluation capabilities according to the visual information they target, rather than their output modality.

source.raw_tex: We introduce \methodname, a shared hierarchy that organizes I2I supervision objectives and I2T evaluation capabilities according to the visual information they target, rather than their output modality.

taxonomy_caption.text: A unified taxonomy of visual tasks organized into three broad families: Recognition, Reconstruction, and Reorganization. Each leaf is explicitly typed as either an I2I supervision objective or an I2T evaluation capability, allowing the two modalities to share the same visual hierarchy without conflating their task identities.

source.raw_tex: A unified taxonomy of visual tasks organized into three broad families: \textit{Recognition}, \textit{Reconstruction}, and \textit{Reorganization}. Each leaf is explicitly typed as either an I2I supervision objective or an I2T evaluation capability, allowing the two modalities to share the same visual hierarchy without conflating their task identities.

taxonomy_annotation.text: Once the capability vocabulary is finalized, we separately assign each I2T benchmark sample to its primary capability leaf. To scale this annotation, three independent LLM judges label each sample according to the finalized taxonomy and annotation guidelines, and the final label is determined by majority vote. A sample is retained when at least two of the three judges agree on its label, and samples without a two-of-three consensus are excluded.

related_example.text: Counting improves with all 17 sources, with 12 gains reaching p<0.05. Object pointing produces the largest observed gain (+3.57 pp, p<0.001): both tasks require identifying the objects to be counted.

cross_results.text: Inpainting improves category recognition (+3.22 pp) and 2D ordering (+11.05 pp), while 2.5D segmentation produces the largest observed ordering gain (+11.58 pp). Colorization gives the largest observed gain on visual correspondence (+5.71 pp), crossing the taxonomy's Reconstruction–Reorganization boundary. All four gains have p<0.01.
